title: One run policy for threads, workers and the GPU

blocks.text: 11.4.6 One Run Policy for Threads, Workers and the GPU

By now GridCap's planning service has settings in many places: one thread for HiGHS so plans repeat (lesson 10.2.2), workers for CP-SAT, a GPU when there is one (lesson 11.4.2), PDLP's tolerance, a gap for the MILP, a method for cuOpt (lesson 11.4.4). Each was decided for a good reason, and each lives next to the call that uses it. The result is a service whose behaviour no one can state in one place, and whose manifest records what the code happened to pass, not what was intended. This lesson gathers every one of those decisions into a single **run policy**: one object, made by one function from the job and the machine, that decides the device, solver, method, threads and tolerance, falls back to the CPU, is written into the manifest, and says how a GPU result may be used for a capital plan. GridCap is a fictional utility; its numbers are teaching data.
The Model
The policy decides how to run the models of this module; it builds none. They are, in brief:

**The capital plan** (lesson 11.4.5), GridCap medium: projects $`i \in P`$, start years $`t \in T_i`$, must-do projects $`M`$, alternative groups $`\mathcal{G}`$, budgets $`B_y`$, spend $`s_{i,t,y}`$ and NPV $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ in $k, and $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$:

\begin{aligned}
\max \;& \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \\
\text{s.t. }& \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} \le 1 \;\; \forall i \in P \setminus M \;\; \text{(once}_i),
\qquad \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} = 1 \;\; \forall i \in M \;\; \text{(must}_i), \\
& \sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} \le 1 \;\; \forall g \in \mathcal{G} \;\; \text{(alt}_g),
\qquad \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} s_{i,t,y}\, x_{i,t} \le B_y \;\; \forall y \in Y \;\; \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}

**Its LP relaxation** (lesson 11.4.1): the same rows with $`0 \le x_{i,t} \le 1`$, here for GridCap small. **The transportation LP** (lesson 11.4.3): $`x_{i,j} \ge 0`$, minimise $`\sum k_{i,j} x_{i,j}`$ subject to $`\text{supply}_i`$ and $`\text{demand}_j`$, here with $`n = 300`$ (90,000 variables, 180,000 nonzeros), standing in for a large LP.
One Object Decides the Device, Solver, Method, Threads and Tolerance
A **job** says what is being solved and what the answer is for. A **run policy** says how to solve it. Both are frozen dataclasses, so a policy cannot be changed after it is made:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Job:
    name: str
    kind: str                   # "lp" or "milp"
    nonzeros: int
    use: str                    # "plan" (the plan of record), "bound" (an LP bound), or "start" (a starting plan)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RunPolicy:
    device: str
    solver: str
    method: str
    threads: int
    tolerance: float            # LP optimality tolerance, or the MILP relative gap
    verify_on_cpu: bool         # a GPU answer is checked on the CPU before anything uses it
    why: str
One function makes the policy, from the job and one fact about the machine:
Each branch carries a reason from this module:

items: **The plan of record never goes to the GPU.** It must repeat bit for bit for the auditor, and HiGHS on one thread does (lessons 10.2.2 and 11.4.5); cuOpt's MILP does not (lesson 11.4.4). A continuous plan of record goes to simplex for the same reason, and because simplex ends on a vertex (lesson 11.4.1).

**A starting plan may come from cuOpt**, with a looser gap, because it will be checked and only handed to the CPU solver as a start. `threads` 0 means cuOpt picks its own CPU workers; HiGHS gets exactly 1.

**A large LP goes to the GPU's PDLP**, a small one stays on the CPU. `GPU_MIN_NONZEROS` is 100,000: on the build machine the GPU first matched the CPU at the 300 × 300 transportation LP (180,000 nonzeros) and lost clearly at 100 × 100 (20,000), lesson 11.4.3.
**Every tolerance is explicit**, so the manifest can record what "optimal" promised.

blocks.text: `decide` is a pure function, so its whole behaviour can be printed for both answers to "is there a GPU?", on any machine:

Two jobs of five change device when a GPU appears; three never do. Every `GPU? False` row is a CPU row, so the service works the same on a machine with no GPU, only without the two GPU branches.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Policy Falls Back to the CPU and Is Recorded in the Manifest

`run` solves a job under the live policy, `decide(job, gpu_available())`, and handles the two fallback triggers of lesson 11.4.2 with the policy itself: if the GPU's PDLP does not answer `Optimal`, it asks `decide` again with `gpu=False` and solves under that CPU policy, so the manifest records the policy that actually ran, not the one first chosen:

policy = decide(job, gpu_available())
    if policy.device == "gpu" and policy.solver == "highs":
        result = highs(m, "pdlp", tolerance=policy.tolerance)
        if result["status"] != "Optimal":                       # the fallback: same job, the CPU branch
            policy = decide(job, gpu=False)
            result = highs(m, policy.method, tolerance=policy.tolerance)

record = {"policy": asdict(policy), "result": {"solver": result["solver"], "status": result["status"],
                                                   "objective": round(result["objective"], 6)}}

The returned record goes into the manifest beside lesson 11.4.4's fields: the policy is the `solver` block, with the reason, and it is the same on every machine that made the same decision. The GridCap small LP relaxation, on any machine:

{"device": "cpu", "solver": "highs", "method": "simplex", "threads": 1, "tolerance": 1e-07, "verify_on_cpu": false, "why": "small LP: the CPU is faster"}
{"solver": "highs-simplex", "status": "Optimal", "objective": 26587.44151}

A GPU Result Serves a Capital Plan Only as a Bound or a Start, Verified on the CPU
Every GPU branch in the policy has `verify_on_cpu` set, and `run` acts on it before anything uses the answer:

if policy.verify_on_cpu and job.kind == "lp":              # a CPU interior point solve, held to 1e-6
        cpu = highs(m, "ipm")
        record["verified_on_cpu"] = relative_difference(result["objective"], cpu["objective"]) <= 1e-6
    elif policy.verify_on_cpu:                                 # a MILP plan: rows, integrality, and the gap
        cpu = highs(m, threads=1, gap=policy.tolerance)        # to the best bound any solver proved (lesson 11.4.5)
        best = min(result["bound"], cpu["bound"])              # a maximisation: the smallest bound is the tightest
        record["verified_on_cpu"] = check(m, result, best, policy.tolerance)[0]

A MILP plan is judged as lesson 11.4.5 judges one: against the tightest bound any solver proved, not against the bound of the solver that found it. So `run` also solves the job with HiGHS on one CPU thread to the same gap, and passes the smaller of the two bounds (the model is a maximisation) to `check`. A cuOpt plan that only met cuOpt's own bound, when HiGHS had proved a tighter one, is refused. cuOpt's plans change from run to run (lesson 11.4.4), so the objective above is one run's.
Why each use is acceptable, and the one that is not:

items: **An LP bound or relaxation.** The relaxation's optimum caps every plan's worth (lesson 3.1.1); analysts use it to say how far a plan is from the best possible. A GPU's PDLP gives it within its tolerance, $`2 \times 10^{-9}`$ here, which is far finer than any budget decision. The CPU interior point confirms it, and the manifest says it was confirmed.

**A starting or heuristic plan.** A cuOpt plan that passes lesson 11.4.5's check (rows kept, integral, within its gap) can be handed to HiGHS as a start (lesson 11.2.1). HiGHS then proves, or improves, the plan on the CPU, and the plan of record is HiGHS's. A start that fails the check is dropped and the CPU solve runs without it.

**The plan of record: never from the GPU.** It must repeat bit for bit and carry a full proof from one solver, and no GPU path in this module repeats a MILP plan. The policy has no branch that sends it there, whatever the machine has.

blocks.text: The rule in one line: **the GPU may make the night shorter, never the plan different.** Everything it produces is either a number the CPU confirms or a start the CPU solver improves on, and every answer a planner signs comes from a run the auditor can repeat.
<!-- practice 2 -->
HiGHS Stays at the Centre of the Policy

This course runs HiGHS as its default solver (the course README says so, and lesson 2.4.1 set it beside GLOP and PDLP). The policy keeps it at the centre on every device: HiGHS's simplex and interior point on the CPU, HiGHS's own GPU PDLP (cuPDLP-C) for a large LP, and HiGHS on one thread for the plan of record. A team that standardises on HiGHS therefore gets the GPU path from the same library, with the same model format, the same status codes and the same version pin, and the CPU fallback is HiGHS too. cuOpt enters only where it is the better tool: a GPU heuristic plan, checked.
Summary

items: **One object decides the device, solver, method, threads and tolerance.** `decide(job, gpu)` is pure and frozen; every `gpu=False` branch is a CPU branch.
**The policy falls back to the CPU and is recorded in the manifest.** A refused GPU answer makes `run` ask the policy again without a GPU, and the record holds the policy that ran.

**A GPU result serves a capital plan only as a bound or a start, verified on the CPU.** The LP bound is confirmed by an interior point solve; a cuOpt plan is checked and then improved by HiGHS; the plan of record never comes from the GPU.
**HiGHS stays at the centre of the policy.** CPU simplex and interior point, GPU PDLP, and the one-thread plan of record all come from HiGHS.

rows: HiGHS PDLP, else HiGHS interior point
small LP, or a continuous plan of record

blocks.text: **Further reading:** HiGHS, [GPU acceleration](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/guide/gpu/) (one library, its PDLP on the GPU with the same `solver` option, and the tolerances to raise for it); NVIDIA cuOpt, [LP and MILP settings](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuopt/user-guide/latest/lp-milp-settings.html) (`num_cpu_threads` chosen from the core count by default, `method`, and the MILP gap); the parameter comments in OR-Tools' [`solvers.proto`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/pdlp/solvers.proto) (`num_threads` and the shard count that reproducible PDLP runs must keep).
Challenges

items: Add a job "what-if for a board meeting, answer in a minute", a MILP whose answer is shown but never signed. Write its branch in `decide` and say what `verify_on_cpu` should be.
Your workstation's GPU is replaced by a larger one. Which line of the policy should change, and what would you run first to change it? (Lesson 11.4.3.)
A teammate wants `decide` to read `gpu_available()` itself instead of taking `gpu` as an argument. What does the module lose?

blocks.text: Design Note: A Policy Is Data, So It Can Be Diffed

Because a policy is a frozen dataclass printed into the manifest, a change of policy shows up as a change of data: two manifests that differ only in `policy.device` tell the auditor exactly why their bits may differ, and a review of `decide` is a review of one function with one table of outputs. The alternative, settings scattered beside each call, has no single place to review and nothing to record.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change. Without a GPU, the GPU branches are shown in the table but not run.

**run_policy.py.** The jobs, the policy for each with and without a GPU, a live run of the GridCap small LP relaxation, and on a GPU the large LP and the starting plan, each verified on the CPU (*One Object Decides*, *The Policy Falls Back*, *A GPU Result Serves a Capital Plan*). *Try:* Lower `GPU_MIN_NONZEROS` to 100 and predict which rows of the table change and what the live GridCap run does on a GPU.
